contrast.b_has_a_lacks: B has long, dense, multi-sentence captions of fine-grained human–object action sequences. The paired captions differ in one detail, such as left/right hand, direction, order of events, added vs. removed, or an object's location. L.name: Fine-grained caption discrimination
L.definition: Mostly "Which caption best describes this video?" with two near-identical long captions that differ in one detail (left/right hand, direction, object, verb, count, gymnastic element). contrast.a_has_b_lacks: A is dominated by caption-matching pairs that are near-identical, differing in one fine-grained detail (left vs right hand, added vs removed, direction, rotating vs not, an object or verb swap). Solving them needs careful temporal and spatial perception of manipulation details.
contrast.b_has_a_lacks: B's captions are movie-clip descriptions that start with a scene location ("In the living room, ...", "On a street, ..."). They differ in who the character is (appearance, gender, clothing), the emotion or manner (defiantly, angrily), or the scene itself. The two options often describe entirely different scenes. Solving them needs character identification, scene setting and affect or intent, not precise hand or motion detail.

L.name: Counterfactual collision reasoning (synthetic physics)
L.definition: Questions about simulated scenes of colored geometric objects (cubes, spheres, cylinders), asking what collision events would or would not happen if an object is removed. Variants ask which events are causally responsible for a collision, or what mass change or stick removal would produce an outcome.

contrast.a_has_b_lacks: A asks counterfactual questions ("if X is removed / without X, what will or won't happen?"). Answering means mentally removing an object and simulating how the collisions change. A also has related causal and intervention items: change a mass to make something move, which collision is responsible, and where fluid would flow. Options are often 3–4 and sometimes non-collision.
contrast.b_has_a_lacks: B asks only predictive questions ("What/Which event will happen next?"). They need extrapolating the observed motion forward, with no hypothetical intervention. The question text is a fixed generic template, and nearly all items have two collision options.

They require fine-grained verification of whole-video temporal order and detail. They draw on long dense captions, gymnastics element lists, lab-procedure steps and "First... Then..." templates.
contrast.b_has_a_lacks: B items are short, targeted questions about one moment, such as "what does X do after/before Y", "at what time does X happen", or yes/no ordering checks. They have distinct short-phrase answer options (often 4–5) and ask for a single action, object or time-range. contrast.a_has_b_lacks: A asks a predictive question ("What will happen next?") that requires forecasting the next collision from the observed motion in the video. It has no counterfactual condition, and the options are always two short collision statements.
contrast.b_has_a_lacks: B asks counterfactual questions ("without/if X is removed, which will (not) happen") that require reasoning about causal dependence between objects. It requires reading the symbols, their order, colour, and spelling, and predicting the next letter. Options are short strings such as "ayxe" or "rectangle, square, triangle". A also has a few off-domain academic items, such as medical and physics questions.
contrast.b_has_a_lacks: B asks about natural everyday and real-world videos. It covers human actions and their sequence, counting repetitions, hand motion direction, why someone does something, who or what a person is, and yes/no checks. Options are natural-language phrases, often 4-6 of them, and the questions are in a mix of lowercase and sentence-case styles.

Answering requires recognizing animal actions, events, temporal order or timestamps, and the causes of behavior.

contrast.a_has_b_lacks: A is centered on animals (dogs, cats, bears, parrots, babies/pets) as the subject, with questions about identifying the animal, describing its behavior or feelings, and whole-video descriptions.
